> INTRODUCTION

South Australia has only 184 species of mosses, so far as is known. The follow-ing discussion of their distribution and geographical affinities is based on the data in 

my moss flora of the State (Catcheside 1980), together with additions and amendments gathered since it was compiled. The names used are those in that book, with minor exceptions. Many species are restricted in distribution to a few favourable habitats, especially in deep and moist gorges. To some extent, the small number in the State flora is due to imperfect exploration and therefore might be augmented by more through searches. Thus a few species (9 in all) are known in the southern mountains (Mac-Donnell Ranges) of the arid zone of the Northern Territory, but not yet in South Australia. Some of these may occur, particularly in the mountains of the North West of the State. Other species are found in both Victoria and Western Australia and a few of these could also be in the State. However, the total number is not likely finally to exceed 200 by very much, nor would any additions greatly affect the general conclusions that can now be drawn about the geographical affinities of the moss flora. The relative impoverishment of the moss flora is due to a number of factors of which aridity is a prominent one. About two thirds of the State enjoys less than 250 mm of rain per annum on the average and even this amount is very erratic in occurrence. Nevertheless the drier areas have a fairly rich moss flora, comprising species able to cope with aridity. Some 45 species are known to extend into areas with under 250 mm of rain per annum. It must be admitted that many are ephemerals and that others favour shel-tered habitats, often more permanently moist, as in gorges.
